answers: The Navy began procuring John Lewis (TAO-205) class oilers in FY2016, and a total of four have been procured through FY2019, including two in FY2019. The first six ships are being procured under a block buy contract that was authorized by Section 127 of the FY2016 National Defense Authorization Act (S. 1356/P.L. 114-92 of November 25, 2015). The Navy wants to procure a total of 20 TAO-205s. The Navy's proposed FY2020 budget requests the procurement of the fifth and sixth ships in the program. The Navy estimates the combined procurement cost of the two ships at $1,056.3 million, or an average of $528.1 million each. The two ships have received $75.0 million in prior-year advance procurement (AP) funding, and the Navy's proposed FY2020 budget requests the remaining $981.2 million in procurement funding needed to complete the two ships' estimated combined procurement cost. The Navy's proposed FY2020 budget also requests $73.0 million in AP funding for TAO-205s to be procured in future fiscal years, and $3.7 million in cost-to-complete procurement funding to cover cost growth on TAO-205s procured in prior fiscal years, bringing the total FY2020 procurement funding request for the TAO-205 program (aside from outfitting and post-delivery costs) to $1,057.9 million. Issues for Congress include the following: whether to approve, reject, or modify the Navy's FY2020 procurement funding request for the TAO-205 program; the number of oilers the Navy will require in coming years to support its operations; and whether to encourage or direct the Navy to build TAO-205s with more ship self-defense equipment than currently planned by the Navy.

**Summary of the John Lewis (TAO-205) Class Oiler Shipbuilding Program Report**

The John Lewis (TAO-205) class oiler shipbuilding program is a key initiative of the U.S. Navy aimed at modernizing its fleet of underway replenishment ships. The program seeks to build 20 new oilers to replace the aging Henry J. Kaiser (TAO-187) class, which has been in service since the 1980s. These new oilers are critical to the Navy’s ability to sustain operations at sea, providing fuel, lubricants, fresh water, and small amounts of dry cargo to surface ships and their embarked aircraft during underway replenishments (UNREPs). The TAO-205 class is designed to support the Navy’s operational needs, particularly in forward-deployed areas such as the Western Pacific and the Indian Ocean/Persian Gulf.

The Navy’s FY2020 budget requests the procurement of the fifth and sixth ships in the TAO-205 program, with a combined estimated procurement cost of $1,056.3 million. The program has already seen the delivery of the first four ships, with the first ship scheduled for completion in November 2020. The TAO-205 class is being built by General Dynamics/National Steel and Shipbuilding Company (GD/NASSCO) in San Diego, and the design incorporates existing technologies and features such as a double-hull structure to prevent oil spills and improve safety.

Congress faces several key decisions regarding the program. First, whether to approve, reject, or modify the Navy’s FY2020 procurement funding request. Second, whether the Navy will require more oilers in the coming years, particularly in light of the Navy’s new operational concept, Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO), which emphasizes a more dispersed and flexible fleet. Third, whether to encourage the Navy to equip TAO-205s with more ship self-defense capabilities, given the renewed strategic competition with countries like China and Russia. The current design includes limited self-defense systems, such as the NIXIE Torpedo Countermeasure System and an Advanced Degaussing System, but does not include missile defense systems like CIWS or SeaRAM.

The program has made progress in stabilizing its design and technology, with all critical technologies matured and the lead ship under construction. However, challenges remain, including delays caused by a flooding incident at GD/NASSCO
